title: Planning a New-Construction Lawn: Sod and Irrigation Together
meta_title: Planning a New-Construction Lawn: Sod & Irrigation
meta_description: Starting from bare dirt on a new build gives you a rare chance to plan sod and irrigation as one project from day one. Here's what to think through.
lede: A new-construction lot starts as a blank slate, which is actually an advantage when it comes to planning a lawn from scratch.
excerpt: Why new construction is a good opportunity to plan sod and irrigation as one project.

sections.heading: Starting From Bare Dirt Simplifies Sequencing
paragraphs: One advantage of a new build is that there's no existing lawn to work around. Irrigation lines can go in first without worrying about disturbing established grass, which is exactly the sequencing that works best for a combined sod and irrigation project.

sections.heading: Grading Matters More on New Construction
paragraphs: New lots often need grading work to establish proper drainage before sod goes down, something an established property typically already has settled. Getting this right at the start avoids water pooling issues once the lawn is in.

sections.heading: An Establishment Plan Can Help a New Lawn Start Strong
paragraphs: New-construction lawns are starting completely from scratch, which is exactly the kind of situation an establishment plan is built for, providing guidance and support through the critical early weeks after sod goes down.

sections.heading: Planning Residential, and Sometimes Commercial, Builds
paragraphs: New-construction lawn work covers both residential and commercial properties, so whether it's a single new home or a larger development, the same basic sequencing logic, irrigation before sod, grading before either, applies.

faqs.q: Is it easier to plan irrigation and sod together on new construction?
faqs.a: Yes. Starting from bare dirt means irrigation lines can go in first without needing to work around an existing lawn.

faqs.q: Does a new lot need grading before sod goes down?
faqs.a: Often, yes. New construction typically needs grading to establish proper drainage, which an established property usually already has.

faqs.q: What does an establishment plan add for a new-construction lawn?
faqs.a: It provides guidance and support through the early weeks after installation, which matters for a lawn starting completely from scratch.
